name: Alleged automated foreign-exchange revenue channel

attribution.legal_posture: FATF reports arrests, alleged conduct, and suspected remittance in a jurisdiction-submitted case study; conviction, final judgment, transaction trail, and general prevalence among DPRK IT workers require separate evidence.

caveats: Monitoring, communications behavior, quota pressure, subcontracting, trading activity, geography, language, and any single signal require corroboration before supporting identity, nationality, sanctions, or misconduct attribution.
Evidence and method class: FATF case study submitted by Japan, describing arrests and suspicions.
Fraudulent employment, general DPRK overseas labor, sanctions evasion, and malicious cyber activity remain analytically distinct unless a cited source expressly connects them.
One case offers a single observation; prevalence among DPRK IT workers requires broader measurement.
Use arrest-stage and suspected-remittance language. Keep account identifiers, transaction selectors, and trading-system details unpublished and out of collection.
Remittance to the DPRK is described as suspected; adjudication status is unreported.
The FATF summary covers a general legal-prohibition context; names, docket records, specific legal prohibition, transaction values, and final judicial outcome remain unreported.
This record is policy, labor-governance, economic, or sanctions-evasion context; person, organization, victim, account, transaction, and incident profiles require separate records.

infrastructure.evidence_method_class: FATF case study submitted by Japan, describing arrests and suspicions
infrastructure.statement: FATF reports that in September 2024 two Japanese individuals were arrested for allegedly conspiring with a DPRK IT worker to use a prohibited automated trading system for foreign-exchange transactions and to register information and open accounts unlawfully. Investigators suspected that proceeds from the transactions were remitted to the DPRK.
sampling_limitations: The FATF summary does not provide names, docket records, the specific legal prohibition, transaction values, or a final judicial outcome.
Remittance to the DPRK is described as suspected, not adjudicated.
One case does not establish the prevalence of automated trading among DPRK IT workers.
